questions.question: Draw the business cycle diagram in words: name the axes, the trend line, the four phases in order, the turning points, and define length and amplitude.
questions.expected_answer: Time runs on the horizontal axis and the level of real output on the vertical axis. A gently rising straight line is the trend line, the economy's long-run growth path, and a wave weaves around it. From the lowest point: the trough, where activity stops falling; the upswing or expansion, with output, incomes, employment and spending all rising; the peak, where activity can rise no further, with capacity strained and prices accelerating; and the downswing or contraction, with activity falling to the next trough. The peak and the trough are the turning points. The length of the cycle is the time from one peak to the next peak (or trough to trough); the amplitude is the vertical distance between the trend line and a peak or trough, measuring the cycle's intensity — the larger the amplitude, the stronger the shock and the longer its effects last. A recession is conventionally recognised after two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP, and a depression is a deep, prolonged recession.

questions.question: Set out the exogenous and endogenous explanations of the business cycle with the school attached to each and its policy conclusion, and then list the four named cycle types with their approximate lengths and drivers.
questions.expected_answer: Exogenous explanations, associated with the monetarists, place the causes outside the market system — droughts, wars, oil shocks, pandemics and above all government's own conduct, such as erratic money supply growth and politically timed budgets. Since markets are seen as stable and self-correcting, the monetarist cure is stable, predictable, rules-based policy. Endogenous explanations, associated with the Keynesians, place the causes inside the market system: sticky prices and wages, and confidence that feeds on itself through the multiplier and the accelerator, so upswings and downswings deepen themselves. Since the instability is built in, government must intervene to lean against the cycle. The four types, shortest to longest: Kitchin cycles of roughly three to five years driven by inventories; Juglar cycles of seven to eleven years driven by machinery and equipment investment; Kuznets cycles of fifteen to twenty years driven by building and construction; Kondratieff waves of forty-five to sixty years driven by technological revolutions. Shorter cycles ride on longer ones.

questions.question: Explain, with dated South African examples, how monetary and fiscal policy smooth the cycle, and evaluate the forecasting toolkit of indicator families, moving averages and extrapolation.
questions.expected_answer: In a downswing the Reserve Bank runs expansionary monetary policy — cutting the repo rate, as in the record low of 3,5 percent in 2020, supported by open-market purchases, the cash reserve requirement and moral suasion — while in an overheating upswing it runs contractionary policy, as in the repo hikes of 2022 and 2023 to bring inflation back inside the three to six percent target band. Fiscal policy works through the budget: in a downswing the Treasury raises spending, cuts taxes and lets the deficit widen so the multiplier magnifies the injection; in a boom it restrains spending and closes the deficit. Automatic stabilisers — progressive income tax and grants/UIF — cushion the cycle with no new decision. Limits: both act with lags, heavy borrowing raises debt-service costs and can crowd out private investment, and demand-side tools cannot fix supply-side faults. Forecasting: leading indicators (new orders, building plans, share prices, confidence) turn before the economy; coincident indicators (retail sales, production) turn with it; lagging indicators (unemployment) turn after it. Moving averages smooth noise to reveal direction; extrapolation projects the path forward but assumes the future repeats the past, which fails exactly at turning points — so indicators give direction, not dates or magnitudes.
